# Bhikkhunī Saṁyutta (SN 5)

**ID:** SN 5
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Bhikkhunī Saṁyutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0301m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bhikkhunī Saṁyutta* (SN 5) is the fifth division of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated within the *Sagāthāvagga* [Bodhi 2003; Bingenheimer]. It consists of ten short suttas in mixed prose and verse, undivided into sub-chapters (*vagga*s) [Bodhi 2003]. All ten discourses adhere to a uniform narrative pattern: an individual Buddhist nun enters the forest to spend the day in solitary meditation, where Māra approaches to disrupt her concentration with seductive questions, taunts, or sexist dismissals of female spiritual capacity (such as in SN 5.2) [Bodhi 2003]. Recognizing Māra, each nun, an enlightened arahant, promptly deflects his wiles with a sharp retort in verse [Bodhi 2003; Collett 2014]. Because of this shared thematic and structural focus, the collection is placed immediately following the *Māra Saṁyutta* [Bodhi 2003; Bingenheimer].

The collection contains thirty-seven verses, several of which overlap with the *Therīgāthā* in the *Khuddakanikāya*, though a substantial number are unique to the saṁyutta [Bodhi 2003]. Certain nuns featured here, such as Vajirā, do not appear in the *Therīgāthā* at all, and verses are sometimes attributed to different figures across traditions [Bodhi 2003; Norman 1983]. Scholars attribute these variations to the separate oral lines of transmission maintained by the *Samyutta-bhāṇaka*s and *Khuddaka-bhāṇaka*s [Bodhi 2003; Norman 1983]. The canonical status of the framing prose introductions has also been debated, as they are absent in the *Therīgāthā* [Norman 1983]. A Sanskrit *uddāna* found in Turkestan matches the contents of the Pali *Bhikkhunī Saṁyutta*, showing that this recension pre-dates the schism between the Theravādins and Sarvāstivādins [Norman 1983]. Early modern translations include Ernst Windisch's German rendering (1895) and Caroline Rhys Davids' English translation [Bingenheimer].

DharmaNexus confirms these cross-language alignments with high-scoring matches in T 100 and T 99, alongside alignments with Sanskrit and Tibetan Vinaya and Abhidharma literature, notably the *Saṅghabhedavastu* and Śamathadeva's *Abhidharmakośopāyikā-ṭīkā* [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records that the text shares the greatest volume of recurring textual material with the *Māra Saṁyutta* (SN 4), followed by the *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22) and the *Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].
